passages.title: Where Is Biscuit?
passages.text:
Hi everyone! This is my second post this week, and it has a happy ending.

On Sunday evening, our neighbour Mrs. Levi knocked on our door. She was crying. Her small brown dog, Biscuit, was missing. She left the garden gate open by mistake, and Biscuit ran out.

My brother and I made posters with Biscuit's photo and put them on trees in our street. We also shared the photo in our building's group chat. For two days, nothing happened. Then, on Tuesday morning, a boy from the next street called. He found Biscuit sleeping under a bench in the park, next to the playground. We ran there with Mrs. Levi. When Biscuit saw her, he jumped into her arms.

Yesterday, Mrs. Levi brought us a big chocolate cake to say thank you. It was delicious! Next time, she says, she will close the gate.

passages.title: A Day Without Cars
passages.text:
Once a year, the small town of Green Hill has a day without cars. On this day, from eight in the morning to six in the evening, no cars or buses can drive in the town centre. People walk, ride bikes or use skateboards. The streets become very quiet, and children can play in the middle of the road.

The idea started five years ago. A group of parents wanted their children to breathe cleaner air. At first, some shop owners were worried. They thought fewer people would come to their shops. But the opposite happened. Many families came to the centre to walk around, and they bought ice cream, books and cold drinks. Now the shop owners help to plan the day.

This year, the town will also offer free bike repairs in the main square. Some people want a car-free day every month.

passages.title: Dina's Kitchen
passages.text:
Dina Peretz is fifteen years old, and she already has her own cooking show on the internet.

It all started when she was eleven. Her grandmother broke her arm and could not cook, so Dina helped her in the kitchen every afternoon. Her grandmother explained each step, and Dina wrote everything in a notebook.

A year later, Dina's older brother filmed her making her grandmother's lentil soup. He put the video online, and thousands of people watched it. Today, Dina makes a new video every Friday. She cooks simple dishes that teenagers can make at home with cheap ingredients.

Dina does not want to be a chef. "I want to be a doctor," she says. "Cooking is my hobby, and it helps me relax after school." Her grandmother is still her biggest fan. She watches every video twice.

passages.title: The Rainy Final
passages.text:
It was the last game of the season, and it was raining hard. Tom's team, the Blue Hawks, needed only one point to win the league. Tom was the goalkeeper. He was nervous, because in the last game he made a big mistake and the other team scored.

In the first half, nobody scored. The ball was heavy and the grass was wet, so the players kept falling. In the second half, the other team's best player ran toward the goal and kicked the ball very hard. Tom jumped to the left and caught it with both hands. His teammates shouted his name.

The game ended 0-0. One point was enough, and the Blue Hawks were the champions. After the game, the coach gave Tom the ball. "You earned this," she said. Tom smiled. He was wet and cold, but he did not care.

passages.title: Phones Off, Heads Up
passages.text:
Last September, our school decided that students must keep their phones in their lockers from the first bell until the last. Many students were angry, and I was one of them. I was sure the new rule would make school boring and stressful. Six months later, I have changed my mind. I believe it is one of the best decisions our school has ever made.

The first change I noticed was during the breaks. Before the rule, the schoolyard was strangely quiet. Everyone sat on benches, looking down at a screen. Now the yard is noisy again. People play basketball, argue about music and even talk to students from other classes. According to the school counsellor, the number of fights that started online has dropped by half since September.

The second change happened in class. Without a phone buzzing in my pocket, I find it much easier to concentrate. My grades in maths have gone up, although I admit that my new private teacher may also be part of the reason.

Of course, the rule is not perfect. Some parents complain that they cannot reach their children during the day. In my opinion, the school office could solve this easily by passing on urgent messages.

Phones are wonderful tools, but we do not need them every minute. Sometimes the best thing a screen can do for us is stay dark.

passages.title: Gardeners Under the Sea
passages.text:
Off the coast of a small fishing village called Port Amari, a group of volunteer divers spends every Saturday working in an unusual garden. The garden is ten metres under the sea, and instead of flowers, they grow coral.

Coral reefs look like colourful rocks, but they are actually made of millions of tiny animals. Reefs are home to about a quarter of all kinds of sea life, even though they cover less than one percent of the sea floor. Sadly, many reefs around the world are dying. When the water becomes too warm, the coral loses its colour and often dies. Scientists call this "bleaching".

The Port Amari project began in 2019, after a storm destroyed much of the local reef. The divers collect small broken pieces of living coral and tie them to metal frames that look like underwater tables. When the pieces have grown large enough, the divers move them back onto the reef.

The work is slow. A piece of coral the size of a finger may need twelve months to grow as big as a hand. Not every piece survives, either: in the first year, almost half of them died. Since then, the divers have learned which kinds of coral grow best in their bay.

Today, fish are slowly returning to the reef, and so are the tourists who come to watch them. "We cannot save every reef," says the project leader, Dalia Moss, "but we can give ours a second chance."

passages.title: Greetings from Lyon
passages.text:
Subject: Greetings from Lyon!

Hi Yoav,

Sorry I haven't written for so long. The last three weeks have been crazy, but in a good way!

As you know, I'm spending the semester at a school in Lyon, France, as part of an exchange programme. I'm staying with the Moreau family. They have two kids: Camille, who is my age, and Hugo, who is eight and never stops asking me questions about Israel. On my first evening, he wanted to know if I ride a camel to school. I told him I take the bus, like him. He looked really disappointed!

School here is very different. Lessons start at eight and finish at five, and lunch takes almost two hours. At first I thought it was a waste of time, but now I love it. Everyone sits together and actually talks. The food is excellent, too, although I still can't get used to eating cheese after every meal.

The hardest part is the language. I studied French for a year before I came, but people speak so fast that I sometimes understand only half. Camille helps me a lot. Every evening we sit together: I help her with her English homework, and she corrects my French.

I'll be back on 20 December. Can we meet during the holiday? I've got a small present for you, but I won't tell you what it is!

Write soon,
Daniel

passages.title: The Runner Who Started Late
passages.text:
Most professional athletes begin training as children. Lena Varga did not run her first race until she was thirty-one.

Lena grew up in a small town, where she later worked as a bank clerk. She describes her younger self as "the girl who always had a note to get out of sports lessons". Everything changed in 2009, when her doctor told her that she needed to lower her blood pressure. He suggested walking for thirty minutes a day. Lena began walking to work instead of taking the tram, and after a few months, she started to jog part of the way.

In 2011, a colleague persuaded her to enter a ten-kilometre charity run. She finished in the top twenty, ahead of many runners who had trained for years. A local coach who saw the race offered to train her for free. Within three years, Lena had moved up to the marathon, and in 2015 she won her country's marathon championship at the age of thirty-five.

Lena never reached the Olympics. A knee injury in 2016 ended her professional career. However, she says she has no regrets. Today she runs a club for adults who have never done any sport before. "People tell me they are too old or too slow," she says. "I tell them that I was both."

passages.title: The Robot at the Library
passages.text:
When the public library in Riverton got a robot last spring, many people expected something from a science-fiction film. Instead, they met Pip: a white machine about one metre tall, with a round screen for a face and two wheels instead of legs.

Pip's main job is to help visitors find books. A visitor can say the title or the name of the writer, and Pip shows on its screen where the book is. Then it rolls slowly to the right shelf and waits there with a little light flashing. Pip can also tell children stories in four languages and remind visitors when their books are due.

The librarians were nervous at first. Some of them worried that the robot would replace them. "That hasn't happened," says head librarian Omar Haddad. "Pip answers the simple questions, like where the toilets are, about two hundred times a day. That gives us more time for the interesting work, such as helping a student with a research project or finding the right book for a child who hates reading."

Pip is not perfect. It cannot climb stairs, so it only works on the ground floor, and it sometimes misunderstands people who speak quickly or quietly. Last month it led an elderly man who was looking for a book about gardens to the section on war history.

Still, visits to the library have risen by fifteen percent since Pip arrived, and the library plans to buy a second robot next year.

passages.title: The Bell of Marrow Bay
passages.text:
Every evening at sunset, someone in Marrow Bay, a fishing town on a rocky northern coast, rings a bronze bell on the cliff above the harbour. Visitors usually assume it is a church bell. In fact, its history is far more practical, and far more tragic.

In the winter of 1781, a sudden storm caught eleven fishing boats outside the harbour. Thick fog came in with the wind, and the fishermen, unable to see the narrow entrance between the rocks, sailed in circles for hours. Only four boats came home. The following spring, the town's widows sold their wedding rings and silver to pay for a bell. On foggy nights, someone would ring it every few minutes until the last boat was safe, so that the sailors could follow the sound.

For generations, the job of bell-ringer passed from parent to child within the Aldren family. The most famous of them, Margit Aldren, is said to have rung the bell for nineteen hours without a break during the great fog of 1852, saving the entire fleet. Whether the story is entirely true is uncertain, since the town's records from that year were lost in a fire. What is certain is that the bell became the town's symbol, appearing on its flag and even on the labels of its tinned fish.

When a lighthouse with an electric foghorn was built in 1968, the bell was no longer needed. The town council voted to take it down and sell it, but the decision caused such anger that it was reversed within a week. Instead, the council agreed that the bell would be rung once a day, at sunset, in memory of those lost at sea.

Today, few residents still fish for a living, and most of the young people have moved to the cities. Yet every evening, someone climbs the cliff path and rings the bell, even when there is no boat in the harbour to hear it.

passages.title: Why Teenagers Can't Fall Asleep
passages.text:
Parents often complain that teenagers stay up too late and then cannot get out of bed in the morning. It is easy to see this as laziness. Sleep researchers, however, argue that the problem is largely biological.

During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts. Melatonin, the hormone that makes us feel sleepy, starts to be released later in the evening than it is in children or adults. As a result, many teenagers simply do not feel tired until eleven o'clock or even midnight. Since most of them still need between eight and ten hours of sleep, an alarm at half past six leaves them in a state of permanent jet lag.

Some schools have started to take this seriously. At Hollins Park, a secondary school that took part in a two-year trial, the first lesson was moved from 8:00 to 9:15. The results surprised even the teachers who had suggested the change. Students slept, on average, forty minutes longer. Fewer of them arrived late, and their marks in morning lessons improved. Perhaps most interestingly, the school nurse reported fewer visits from students complaining of headaches and stress.

Not everyone was convinced. Some parents found it difficult to organise their own working day around the new timetable, and the sports teams had to train later in the afternoon, when it was already getting dark in winter. Critics also point out that a single school is not enough evidence. The students at Hollins Park knew they were part of an experiment, and this alone may have changed their behaviour.

Still, the trial raises an uncomfortable question. If we know that teenage brains work on a different schedule, why do we continue to design the school day around the needs of adults?

passages.title: Let the Algorithm Rest
passages.text:
I used to discover music by accident: a song on a friend's mixtape, a band playing in the corner of a café, a CD with a strange cover that I bought because I liked the colours. Most of those accidents were disappointing. A few changed my life.

Today, my phone discovers music for me. Every Monday, a streaming app presents a playlist that it claims was "made just for you", and the frightening thing is that it usually is. The algorithm knows that I like sad piano songs in the evening and loud guitars when I go running. It is rarely wrong. And that, I have come to believe, is exactly the problem.

An algorithm learns from what we have already enjoyed, so it tends to offer more of the same. It is excellent at giving us what we want and terrible at giving us what we did not know we wanted. Over time, our taste does not grow. It gets narrower, like a path that is walked so often that the grass on either side disappears.

Supporters of streaming will reply that never in history has so much music been so easy to reach, and they are right. A teenager in a small village can listen to the same rare jazz recording as a professor in New York. But access is not the same as discovery. Having a library card does not make anyone a reader.

I am not suggesting that we delete our apps. I still use mine every day. But once a week, I try to choose something the algorithm would never pick for me: a radio station from another country, an album recommended by my grandmother, a style of music I am sure I hate. Most of the time, I am right about it. Occasionally, I am wonderfully wrong.

passages.title: The Projector
passages.text:
The Rex Cinema had been closed for eleven years when Michal found the key. It was in a biscuit tin in her grandfather's garage, tied to a paper label in his small, careful handwriting: Rex, side door.

Her grandfather had been the cinema's projectionist for forty years. As a child, Michal had spent Friday afternoons in his tiny room at the back of the hall, watching dust dance in the beam of light while he changed the heavy reels. When the Rex closed, unable to compete with the multiplex in the new shopping centre, he stopped talking about films altogether. He died the following spring.

The side door opened more easily than she expected. Inside, the seats were covered in grey sheets, and the air smelled of damp carpet. But the projection room was exactly as she remembered it. The old machine stood under a plastic cover, and beside it, on a shelf, were six metal film cans, each labelled with a date and the words "for Michal".

It took her three months, and the help of a retired engineer she found online, to make the projector work again. When the first images finally flickered across the torn screen, she understood. The cans did not contain feature films. They contained hours of home movies: her mother as a teenager, her grandparents dancing at a wedding, and, again and again, a small girl in a red coat sitting in the front row of an empty cinema, laughing at cartoons.

Last month, the Rex opened its doors for one night. Three hundred people from the town came, many of whom had had their first date in those seats. Michal did not show a new blockbuster. She showed her grandfather's films, and for two hours nobody looked at a phone.

title.he: איך ניגשים ל־unseen ומוצאים את הרעיון המרכזי
title.en: Approaching an Unseen Text: the Main Idea

lessons.goal: לדעת איך לקרוא קטע לא מוכר בצורה מסודרת ולמצוא את הרעיון המרכזי שלו.

blocks.he: ב־unseen לא צריך להבין כל מילה. המטרה היא לענות על השאלות, ולכל תשובה יש הוכחה בקטע. קוראים בשלבים, ולא נבהלים ממילים לא מוכרות.

head: שלב
מה עושים
rows: קוראים את הכותרת ומנחשים על מה הקטע.
עוברים על השאלות לפני הקריאה, כדי לדעת מה מחפשים.
קוראים את כל הקטע ברצף, בלי לעצור על כל מילה.
לכל שאלה חוזרים לחלק המתאים בקטע ומחפשים הוכחה.

blocks.he: הרעיון המרכזי הוא מה שכל הקטע אומר יחד, לא פרט אחד
blocks.pattern: main idea = what the whole text is about

blocks.he: איפה מחפשים? בדרך כלל בכותרת, במשפט הראשון ובפסקה האחרונה. גם מילה שחוזרת שוב ושוב בקטע רומזת על הנושא.
blocks.en: Look at the title, the first sentence, the last paragraph and repeated words.

items.en: Our town has a new bike path. It goes from the station to the beach. Many people now ride to work.
items.he: הרעיון המרכזי: שביל האופניים החדש בעיר.

items.en: Bees visit flowers. They carry pollen from one plant to another. Without bees, many fruits would not grow.
items.he: הרעיון המרכזי: הדבורים חשובות לצמחים ולפירות.

blocks.wrong: Main idea: The bike path goes to the beach.
blocks.right: Main idea: The town has a new bike path that many people use.
blocks.he: טעות נפוצה היא לבחור פרט נכון מהקטע. הוא נכון, אבל הוא לא מה שכל הקטע מדבר עליו.
כדי לבדוק תשובה של main idea, אפשר לשאול: האם התשובה הזאת מתאימה לכל הפסקאות, או רק לאחת מהן? אם רק לאחת, זה פרט.

lessons.goal: להבין מה הטקסט אומר בלי לומר במפורש, ולמצוא את הרמזים שמוכיחים את זה.

blocks.he: לפעמים הכותב/ת לא אומר/ת משהו ישירות, אבל נותן/ת רמזים. להסיק (infer) פירושו לחבר את הרמזים ולהגיע למסקנה. בשאלות כאלה מופיעות מילים כמו probably, suggest, we can understand, what does the writer mean.

blocks.pattern: clue in the text + logic = inference

head: Clue
Inference
rows: She checked her watch for the fifth time.
He left the restaurant without finishing his food.
He did not like the food, or he was in a hurry.
The streets were wet and people carried umbrellas.
It was raining or had just rained.

items.en: Dana smiled when she opened the letter, then called her mother right away.
items.he: אפשר להסיק שבמכתב היו חדשות טובות.

items.en: Nobody in the class had heard of the new teacher before.
items.he: אפשר להסיק שהמורה חדש/ה בבית הספר.

blocks.wrong: He left without finishing his food, so he was sick.
blocks.right: He left without finishing his food, so maybe he did not like it or was in a hurry.
blocks.he: מסקנה צריכה להיות מבוססת על הטקסט. תשובה שנשמעת הגיונית בחיים, אבל אין לה רמז בקטע, היא טעות.
לפני שבוחרים תשובה, כדאי למצוא בקטע את המילים שמוכיחות אותה. אם אי אפשר להצביע על רמז, כנראה זו לא התשובה. מילים כמו but, yet, still מסמנות לעיתים קרובות רמז חשוב.

lessons.goal: לזהות למה מתייחסות מילים כמו it, they, this ו־which בטקסט.

blocks.he: כדי לא לחזור על אותה מילה, האנגלית משתמשת במילות הפניה. כדי להבין את הטקסט צריך לדעת על מי או על מה הן מדברות. בדרך כלל התשובה נמצאת לפני המילה, במשפט הקודם או באותו משפט.

head: Word
מתייחס ל...
rows: דבר או רעיון שלם שהוזכר קודם

blocks.he: בודקים את התשובה: מחליפים את המילה בתשובה וקוראים שוב
blocks.pattern: They decided to stay. → The players decided to stay.

items.en: The students planted trees. They watered them every day.
items.he: They = the students, them = the trees

items.en: Parents cannot call their kids during class. The office could solve this.
items.he: this = הבעיה שהורים לא יכולים להתקשר

blocks.wrong: Tom gave the ball to his brother. He was happy. (He = the ball)
blocks.right: He = Tom or his brother. The ball cannot be happy.
blocks.he: לא בוחרים אוטומטית את שם העצם הקרוב ביותר. בודקים גם מספר (יחיד או רבים), מין, והאם זה הגיוני.
בעברית לפעמים משמיטים את הנושא ("הלכתי"), אבל באנגלית תמיד יש נושא. לכן יש באנגלית הרבה מילות הפניה, וכדאי לעצור ולשאול: מי זה?
